comparator.name: Literature and Society
comparator.sourceNotes: The adopted 2026–2027 regulations and Study Guide establish three 60 EC years in the English track. Year one includes literary analysis, theory, language, creative writing and adaptation. The diagnostic test and academic orientation carry no additional credits. The binding study advice requires at least 42 EC and both first-year Academic Skills courses. Year two includes one 3 EC language option, Pronunciation or Presentation. Year three includes 30 EC of approved open study, one two-course specialisation (12 EC), Career Orientation (6 EC), and an individual thesis including its colloquium (12 EC). Changing World 1 requires passing Literary Theory; Changing World 2 requires participation in the first course. Spring thesis entry requires passing all first- and second-year courses. The regulations specify a separate autumn entry rule. The English and Dutch tracks have separate curricula.

core: Close reading, genre and literary analysis across textual forms
Literary theory: multiple critical perspectives (humanist, feminist, Marxist, psychoanalytic) applied to interpretation
Literature's relationship to society, culture and everyday social life
Text-image and text-screen relationships: adaptation, film and visual culture
World and historical literary traditions from ancient texts to contemporary forms
The English-track literary-critical specialisation "Literature in a Changing World"
Creative writing practice across life narrative, poetry and performance; depth differs by track
Scriptwriting, podcasting and intermedial/adapted storytelling across media
Authorial style and voice, with dedicated practice differing by track
Literary-historical grounding for creative practice, from the Middle Ages to the present
adjacent: Language, style and linguistic choice in meaning-making
Publishing, editing and the professional literary/cultural field
questions: How does literature and storytelling respond to and shape contemporary social challenges?
What makes a story or text powerful, and how do creative and rhetorical choices in form and language shape its effect on an audience?
How is meaning produced across text, image and adapted media, and how do adaptations reshape stories for new audiences and forms?

alternatives.label: Literary studies, theory and cultural interpretation
alternatives.concept: Use close reading, literary theory, world myth and a broad literary survey to interpret texts across genres and periods. Study life writing and film adaptation, then draw on art history, visual analysis and environmental media to examine how stories acquire meaning in different cultures.
alternatives.labelReason: Names the actual literary study and the distinct interpretive or creative/public-rhetorical emphasis, without claiming complete specialist or Dutch-track equivalence.
progression: Introductory literary studies precede research in literary theory and film adaptation. Art history moves from a survey to the Renaissance and modern art, then to art historiography.

alternatives.label: Literature, creative practice and public rhetoric
alternatives.concept: Use literary theory and stylistics to interpret texts, write life narratives and experiment with poetry, sound and performance. Develop public speaking through community rhetoric and use media analysis to inform a short documentary project.
alternatives.labelReason: Names the actual literary study and the distinct interpretive or creative/public-rhetorical emphasis, without claiming complete specialist or Dutch-track equivalence.
progression: Introductory literary studies and film analysis come first. Introductory rhetoric precedes stylistics and the applied community-speaking course. Literary theory, the creative laboratory and documentary build on earlier work.
alternatives.distinctness: 5 courses (37.5 EC) differ each way. The primary uses intercultural/mind philosophy, media archaeology, environmental media analysis, Renaissance and museum interpretation; the related direction instead uses philosophy of emotion, modern sociology, contemporary media, oral community rhetoric and documentary production. Literary theory is retained in both. These are actual changes in disciplinary objects and production practice, not claims that companion social science supplies creative-writing craft.

candidates.label: Literature, creative practice and public rhetoric

routeSelection.basis: The normalized target names no specific route. "Literature and Society: English" shares the parent programme's own name and its academic core is literary-critical analysis and literature-and-society content, directly continuing the generic programme's stated identity, while "Creatief Schrijven Nederlands" is explicitly marketed as a distinct, more specialised creative-writing professional track.

selection.assessment: Both options contain six literature courses. Literary stylistics, rhetoric and a poetry workshop add to the shared core. The first option adds four art history courses, media archaeology and environmental media. The second adds applied community speaking, media representation and short documentary, with philosophy of emotion and sociology of modernity as companion study. English literary periods, postcolonial literature, global English, publishing and the required individual thesis remain gaps. The Dutch creative-writing sequence is a separate comparator direction. A third specialist option in publishing, scriptwriting or postcolonial literature lacks a sustained UCR course sequence.

blocks: Partial curricular relationship. Both introduce close reading and the analysis of literary form across poetry, fiction and drama, with the critical terminology of literary analysis; VU frames the course around English literature.
Both apply literary theory, including feminist and Marxist criticism, to interpretation. UCR also studies psychoanalytic, humanist and cultural-minority perspectives.

Partial overlap in selfhood across Western and Buddhist thought. VU teaches intercultural philosophical method and critiques Eurocentric reason across cultures; UCR primarily studies mind, consciousness and personal identity.

Partial curricular relationship. Both analyse how cultural texts expose injustice, support resistance and emancipation, and imagine better futures; VU studies literary texts across several centuries, whereas UCR studies film, photography, music and podcasts in relation to race in American history.

The selected UCR programmes do not include a course on contemporary literature and globalization. Modern History covers political and economic history since 1815 without literary texts, and World Myth & Literature compares ancient myth across cultures rather than literature in a globalized world.
Both examine how adaptation changes a literary or dramatic text. VU focuses on Shakespeare; UCR studies adaptation across works and film genres.

Partial curricular relationship. Both train ecocritical analysis of how texts and images represent relations between humans, nonhuman others and the environment; VU applies this to early modern literature (1550-1700), while UCR applies it to modern visual and audiovisual media.
Partial curricular relationship. Both study life-writing genres (autobiography, memoir, diary, travel narrative and blog) and their theory, and both include students' own writing of life narratives.

Partial curricular relationship. Both combine close reading of writers' formal techniques with a workshop in which students draft, receive feedback on and revise their own creative work; UCR's course centres on poetry, performance and experimental forms.

Partial curricular relationship. Both analyse how linguistic choices at sentence and discourse level, such as stance, modality and cohesion, shape meaning; VU applies this to students' own academic English writing and editing, whereas UCR's stylistics course analyses mainly literary texts.

Partial curricular relationship. Both train students to shape their own texts for specific audiences and purposes by adapting structure, style and register; UCR approaches this through classical and modern rhetoric and does not cover the translation and editing parts of the VU course.
VU studies publishing and editorial production in a dedicated course.

Partial curricular relationship. Both study how cultural objects are made, valued, preserved and passed on, with art history as a shared discipline; VU spans antiquity to the present across several disciplines, while UCR focuses on Western painting from the late Middle Ages onward and its institutions.
Literary history, specialisation and English studies
No dedicated modern American literary-history course. Great Literary Works adds a broad historical literary survey; Media & Race and Histories of Gender study other cultural/historical objects.
The selected UCR programmes do not include a course dedicated to British literary history; related broad literary-survey content, where present, is distributed elsewhere.
VU focuses on transatlantic travel writing. UCR covers travel narrative within a broader study of life writing.

The selected UCR programmes do not include a course on the eighteenth-century novel or women's writing. Histories of Gender studies gender in nineteenth- to twenty-first-century American history, not literary analysis of the novel.
The selected UCR programmes do not include a sociolinguistics or global-English course; UCR offers no equivalent study of English as a global language.

The selected UCR programmes do not include a course on African or postcolonial literature. Media & Race studies race and power in American media, not short stories and comics from the African continent and diaspora.
VU studies Caribbean and postcolonial writing and includes a student research symposium.
Academic skills, language, formation and elective space

Partial curricular relationship. Both teach core academic skills: defining a research focus, finding and using academic sources, and structuring an argued essay; VU's module is a literary-studies research-writing module using MLA citation, while UCR's course also covers personal, ethical and civic development.

No separate scheduled counterpart for this continuation of literary research writing. PPD supplies general academic formation; qualitative social research is not literary source/close-reading methodology.
This is a compulsory academic-English language module; UCR's English-medium curriculum has no equivalent standalone component.
This is a compulsory academic-English language module; UCR's English-medium curriculum has no equivalent standalone component.
VU assigns one English language option. UCR develops oral delivery through rhetoric.

This is a compulsory career-orientation module graded complete/incomplete (strengths, professional profiles, networking, CVs and interviews); no scheduled UCR course is dedicated to career preparation, and Personal & Professional Development is aligned with Academic Skills 1.
VU requires an individual thesis and colloquium. UCR’s optional independent research is outside the scheduled 180 EC.
VU reserves 30 EC for approved open study.

notes.text: Both options develop close reading, literary theory, stylistics and adaptation. VU devotes more coursework to English literary periods, postcolonial literature, global English, translation and publishing. VU requires a 12 EC individual thesis. UCR’s optional independent research is outside the scheduled 180 EC.

The creative option combines life writing and experimental poetry with public speaking and a short documentary. VU’s separate Dutch track has a longer sequence in Dutch literature and creative writing, including fiction and scriptwriting.

audience.programmeDescription: VU Literature and Society studies how literary texts shape and respond to culture and society. The English track combines close reading and theory with English literary history, language, creative writing and publishing, followed by a specialisation and individual thesis. A separate Dutch track concentrates on creative writing and Dutch literature.
audience.comparisonExplanation: Both UCR options include six literature courses. One emphasizes literary interpretation and visual culture. The other adds practice in life writing, poetry, public speaking and documentary. VU provides more specialist English literary history, language and publishing study, and requires an individual thesis.
